newsitem.title: USA: Sallie Mae CEO aims to break deadlock by resigning.
newsitem.headline: Sallie Mae CEO aims to break deadlock by resigning.

text.p: The battle for control of the Student Loan Marketing Association appeared headed for a compromise Wednesday with the announcement by its chief executive that he will resign.

Lawrence Hough, who is also president of Sallie Mae, said he would step down to "break the deadlock" that has prevented management and an opposition group from getting a majority of shareholders to back their competing plans for the company.
Sallie Mae is the nation's largest source of funding for college and other higher education loans. It said Hough will remain with the company through a transition and until a successor is named.
The news sparked a jump in Sallie Mae shares, which rose $6.125 to $126.375 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.

After Sallie Mae's board in January approved moves to end its ties to the federal government, management has been sparring with a group headed by Albert Lord, a former chief operating officer of the company. The dispute goes back to 1994, when Lord left Sallie Mae, citing differences with management.
Both management and Lord's group have been seeking to end government ties for Sallie Mae, which is stockholder-owned and government-sponsored.

But the two sides have differed on business strategy, with the opposition group advocating a major role for the company as an originator of student loans. Sallie Mae has said that making loans could hurt its relationships with hundreds of banks.
Since the 1970s, Sallie Mae has bought federally subsidised and guaranteed loans from banks and other lenders and provided financing to state student loan agencies.
A group of eight directors from Lord's group was elected to the Sallie Mae board in 1995.

Sallie Mae said Tuesday that David Vitale, a vice chairman of First Chicago NBD Corp. and a Sallie Mae director for 20 years, has been proposed to become non-executive chairman. It said it was proposing a slate with 10 nominees and room for five nominees to be named by Lord's group for a July vote that will also decide the issue of ties to the government.
But the Lord group said it was not intererested in being in a minority position on a slate headed by Vitale.

In an interview, Vitale said some banks have already backed away from the company. He said it had missed out on $250 million of business this quarter because of the dispute between management and the opposition group.

One key problem for Sallie Mae has been the Clinton administration's decision a few years ago to shift government involvement in student loans from subsidies and guarantees to direct lending. The government now has about a third of the market.

Sallie Mae's stock tumbled from $75 to $31 around 1993 before it began recovering in 1994. Although some of the recovery has been attributed to Republican gains in Congress and a belief that government would back off, Lord's group and Sallie Mae management have both claimed credit for pursuing business strategies that have lifted the stock.

Hough, who has been chief executive since 1990, said that to resolve the situation, it will be necessary to turn to a chief executive "who draws from a non-government-sponsored enterprise background and experience."

Thomas O'Donnell at Smith Barney Inc. said he reiterated a "buy" on the stock with a near-term target of $140 a share. But he said a government intent on closing its budget gap could squeeze loans and guarantees, which would crimp Sallie Mae's profits.
